neighbours.label: Hedging main verb 'appears/seems/seemed' right after a subject in news or analysis prose (the subject's state is reported as an impression, not a fact)
fire: With exports slowing, Beijing now appears willing to soften its stance.
After two long years of campaigning, many voters seem tired of politics.
The new coach seems determined to rebuild the defence from scratch.
Since the merger, the bank appears to be losing younger customers.
Several of the smaller parties seemed eager to join the coalition.
For the moment, the regulator appears content to wait and watch.
Younger buyers in the city seem uninterested in large cars.
By the third week, the rebels seemed unable to hold the town.
quiet: With exports slowing, Beijing has softened its stance on trade.
After two long years of campaigning, many voters stayed home.
The new coach plans to rebuild the defence from scratch.
Since the merger, the bank has lost many younger customers.
Several of the smaller parties agreed to join the coalition.
For the moment, the regulator will wait for more data.
Younger buyers in the city rarely purchase large cars.
By the third week, the rebels had lost control of the town.

predictions: 'appears'/'seem(s)'/'seemed' after a subject reach 0.4-1.0; the same subjects with a plain verb or copula stay under 0.25.
notes: Probe: 'the government now appears to be ready' 1.040 vs 'is now ready' 0.219 (' now'); 'investors seem worried' 0.548 vs 'are worried' 0.088; 'company seemed intent' 0.447; 'arrived in parliament on Tuesday' 0.417 (weekday after an arrival leaks, kept out of the near misses); 'Suddenly,' 0.090. Card: ' seemed/appears/seem/seems' 12 of top 32, plus ' and', ' Monday'. Suppresses ' able/ready/aware', the adjectives such a verb introduces.
